title: A scoping survey of ChatGPT in mathematics education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly emerging literature on ChatGPT in mathematics education and asks what the reported benefits and challenges are for teachers’ and students’ teaching and learning. Rather than studying a single classroom intervention, the authors conduct a scoping review of research published between November 2022 and May 2024, using Google Scholar, Web of Science, arXiv, HAL, conference proceedings, and snowball sampling to identify relevant work.

The paper focuses on ChatGPT and closely related GPT-based models as tools for mathematics education, but it also includes some studies from broader educational contexts when they are relevant to mathematics teaching and learning. The review covers a wide range of uses: mathematical problem solving, lesson planning, assessment and feedback, personalized learning, critical thinking, collaboration, and attitudes toward AI use. The literature spans primary, secondary, and tertiary contexts, with a substantial emphasis on teachers, pre-service teachers, and students in higher education, though the review also discusses K-12 and specifically middle-school-relevant mathematics topics.

The authors conclude that ChatGPT shows promise as a supplementary support for mathematical explanations, planning, feedback, and personalized assistance, but its performance is inconsistent and often unreliable on more complex mathematical tasks. They highlight recurring concerns about hallucinations, inaccurate reasoning, over-reliance, and the need for human oversight. Overall, the paper argues that ChatGPT should be treated as a helpful but limited tool whose educational value depends on careful prompting, critical evaluation, and pedagogically informed use.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a scoping review/editorial synthesis rather than a primary causal study. It is systematically conducted and peer-relevant, but the evidence base is heterogeneous and largely consists of early qualitative, descriptive, and small experimental studies.
impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests potentially meaningful uses of ChatGPT in mathematics education, but the underlying evidence is mixed and often small-scale. Reported benefits are promising yet unclear in magnitude for general K-12 populations, so the overall impact remains modest/uncertain.

interventions.use_case: scoping review of ChatGPT use in mathematics education as a conversational AI tutor/assistant for student learning, teacher lesson planning, feedback, assessment, and collaborative support

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesized studies showing both promise and limitations for mathematics learning. ChatGPT/LLMs performed well on simple arithmetic, algebraic expressions, and some undergraduate-level tasks, but struggled with more complex problems, graduate-level difficulty, geometry misconceptions, and proof reasoning; for example, Dao and Le (2023) reported performance dropping from 82% on knowledge-level items to 10% on harder items, and Pardos and Bhandari (2024) found human-authored hints produced substantially and statistically significantly higher learning gains than ChatGPT hints across elementary and intermediate algebra.
finding.measure: Accuracy on mathematics and logic problems; exam-item performance; learning gains from hints; correctness of geometry/proof responses

finding.finding_summary: The review reported that ChatGPT could support critical thinking, reasoning, reflection, and collaboration, but also raised concerns that over-reliance might weaken these skills. Evidence included improved computational thinking and self-efficacy in a programming course (n=45; experimental group n=21), improved reflective planning and lesson-analysis skills for pre-service teachers, and better collaborative engagement in group work, alongside warnings that students may accept outputs uncritically or be less inclined to develop independent reasoning.
finding.measure: Computational thinking, programming self-efficacy, motivation, reflective planning quality, collaboration/process quality

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT was associated with improved motivation, engagement, and positive attitudes toward mathematics or AI-supported learning. For example, Yilmaz and Yilmaz (2023) reported significantly higher motivation in the ChatGPT-supported experimental group (n=21) versus control, and the review also notes positive attitudes among students and teachers, though with concerns about over-reliance and ethics.

The review found that ChatGPT could reduce teacher workload by assisting with lesson planning, generating instructional materials, providing feedback, and automating or semi-automating assessment. In the hint-comparison study, 70% of ChatGPT hints passed manual quality checks, indicating practical utility, although human-authored hints still produced significantly larger learning gains; overall, the efficiency value was framed as immediate feedback and faster creation of plans/materials rather than fully reliable automation.
finding.measure: Lesson-plan generation quality, feedback generation, automated scoring, teacher time/workload implications

finding.finding_summary: The paper discussed broader institutional implications for AI adoption in mathematics education, including integrity, privacy, bias, and the need for human oversight in assessment. These are not measured effects but synthesized concerns and policy-relevant implications from the literature, including cautions that ChatGPT may amplify inequities or weaken assessment fairness without governance safeguards.
